stem: An adult with type 1 diabetes uses rapid-acting insulin with meals and an individualized insulin-to-carbohydrate ratio (ICR). Which statement by the client shows correct understanding?

options.A: I use my prescribed ICR to match prandial insulin to the carbohydrate in the meal, while following my plan for any separate correction.
options.B: I use my prescribed ICR with the premeal glucose value to choose the prandial insulin dose, even when the meal's carbohydrate amount changes.
options.C: I use the same prandial insulin dose when meal carbohydrate changes, then use the ICR only if the postmeal glucose is above target.
options.D: I use the ICR to set a maximum carbohydrate amount for each meal, rather than to match the prandial insulin dose to carbohydrate eaten.

rationale: Current ADA Standards of Care recommend teaching most adults with type 1 diabetes to match mealtime insulin doses to carbohydrate intake and, when relevant to the individualized plan, the glycemic effects of fat and protein. ADA insulin-treatment tables describe mealtime insulin dosing based on an insulin-to-carbohydrate ratio, while correction insulin is based on factors such as concurrent glucose, insulin sensitivity, and target glucose. Therefore A correctly describes the ICR as a tool for matching prandial insulin to meal carbohydrate while preserving a separate individualized correction plan. B incorrectly substitutes premeal glucose for carbohydrate intake in the ICR. C disconnects the meal dose from changing carbohydrate intake. D misrepresents the ICR as a carbohydrate-restriction limit rather than an insulin-matching tool.
educational_objective: Use an individualized insulin-to-carbohydrate ratio to match prandial insulin to meal carbohydrate intake, while following the prescribed plan for any separate correction based on current glycemia and other individualized factors.
source_organization: American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee for Diabetes
source_document_title: 9. Pharmacologic Approaches to Glycemic Treatment: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
source_locator: Recommendation 9.3: educate most adults with type 1 diabetes to match mealtime insulin doses to carbohydrate intake and, depending on needs/preferences, fat and protein; teach correction-dose modification based on concurrent glycemia, glycemic trends, sick-day management, and anticipated physical activity. Insulin-treatment tables: mealtime insulin may be based on ICR and correction insulin on ISF and target glucose; with accurate carbohydrate counting, ICR is adjusted when postmeal glucose is consistently out of target.
source_claim_supported: For adults with type 1 diabetes using flexible prandial insulin, the insulin-to-carbohydrate ratio is used to match mealtime insulin to carbohydrate intake, while correction dosing is individualized using current glycemia and related factors.

supporting_sources.organization: American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee for Diabetes
supporting_sources.document_title: 5. Facilitating Positive Health Behaviors and Well-being to Improve Health Outcomes: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
supporting_sources.locator: Recommendation 5.27 and Eating/Meal Plan Approaches and Methods: teach the glycemic impact of carbohydrate tailored to the insulin plan; people using mealtime insulin need education coupling insulin administration with carbohydrate intake; teaching insulin-to-carbohydrate ratios can help modify insulin dosing from meal to meal.
supporting_sources.claim_supported: Carbohydrate counting and insulin-to-carbohydrate ratios can be used to adjust mealtime insulin dosing from meal to meal.

blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, printed pp. 38–39: educate client about medications; educate client on medication self-administration procedures; perform calculations needed for medication administration; prepare and administer medications using rights of medication administration.
blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — individualized prandial insulin self-management
correction_summary: Rebuilt all four statements to remove the very long keyed answer, absolute-word cueing, and implausible distractors. The corrected item isolates the role of the insulin-to-carbohydrate ratio and contrasts it with realistic misconceptions about premeal glucose, fixed prandial dosing, and carbohydrate restriction.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Type 1 diabetes — carbohydrate counting and prandial insulin matching
audit_findings.stem: PASS — specifies adult type 1 diabetes, rapid-acting mealtime insulin, and an individualized ICR without requiring an unstated dose formula.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS — correctly states the role of the ICR and preserves the separate individualized correction component; uniquely best.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS as distractor — plausibly confuses the ICR with a correction factor but incorrectly substitutes premeal glucose for meal carbohydrate.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS as distractor — a fixed prandial dose despite changing carbohydrate intake conflicts with flexible ICR-based dosing.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS as distractor — plausibly confuses carbohydrate counting with carbohydrate restriction; ICR is used to match insulin to carbohydrate intake.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — only A correctly describes both the carbohydrate-matching role of the ICR and the distinct correction component.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — B confuses ICR with correction dosing, C ignores carbohydrate variation, and D converts an insulin-matching tool into a dietary limit.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — option lengths are closely matched; the correct answer is neither uniquely longest nor marked by absolute wording.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — NCSBN Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies directly includes medication teaching, self-administration, and medication calculations.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether B could be defended because current glycemia can influence the total mealtime dose; ADA separates carbohydrate-based ICR dosing from correction dosing based on glycemia, so B remains incorrect and A remains uniquely best.
